usage: Time word; usually goes before the verb.
Combine with a time word to be specific.
Doubling it adds emphasis, like 'day after day'.
examples: Basic habit sentence; 매일 before the object is fine too.
Our dog goes for a walk every day.
Works with any daily routine verb.
nuance: 매일 means 'every day' and is one of the most common time words for talking about routines. It almost always comes before the verb. For other intervals you swap the first part: 매주 (every week), 매달 (every month), 매년 (every year).
mistakes: Saying 매일에 — 매일 does not take 에. Just say 매일.
Confusing 매일 (every day) with 하루 (one day / a day) — they are different.

usage: Polite way to put something off.
nuance: 나중에 means 'later' at some vague, unspecified future time, not necessarily the same day. If you mean 'a little later today', use 이따가 instead. 나중에 is great for politely deferring something without committing to a time.
mistakes: Using 나중에 when you mean 'in a little while today' — that is 이따가.
Dropping 에: the adverb is 나중에, not just 나중.

usage: Short time later, but still today.
Casual; you expect to meet again soon.
이따 is the common shortened form.
I'll call you in a bit
Promising to call soon, same day.
examples: Let's have lunch together in a bit.
I'll come back in a little while.
See you at the cafe in a bit.
nuance: 이따가 means 'a little later today' — a short gap that is still within the same day. Compare with 나중에 (vague 'later', maybe another day) and 이제 (now/from now). In speech people very often shorten 이따가 to 이따.
mistakes: Using 이따가 for next week or 'someday' — for that use 나중에.
Confusing 이따가 (later today) with 있다가 (after staying/being) — different words, same sound.

usage: Native Korean word, same idea as 항상.
언제나 and 늘 are close synonyms.
examples: That restaurant always has a lot of people.
nuance: 늘 means 'always' and is almost interchangeable with 항상. 늘 feels a touch softer and warmer, so it is common in friendly wishes like 늘 행복하세요. Both go right before the verb.
mistakes: Spelling it 늘다 — that is a verb ('to increase'). The adverb is just 늘.
Trying to add a particle (늘에/늘은) — adverbs like 늘 take no particle.

usage: Marks a shift from before to now.
examples: I know a little Korean now.
From now on I'll exercise every day.
nuance: 이제 means 'now', but with the nuance of a change from a previous state ('not until now, but now'). Plain 지금 just points to the present moment with no such contrast. Use 이제 when something is finally different than before.
mistakes: Treating 이제 and 지금 as identical — 지금 is neutral 'right now', 이제 implies a change.
Saying 이제에 — no 에. Just 이제 or 이제부터.

examples: Sorry for being late every time.
That store was closed every time.
Thank you for helping me every time.
nuance: 매번 means 'every time / each time' an event happens, focusing on repeated occasions rather than calendar days. Use 매일 for 'every day' (calendar), but 매번 when something recurs each time a situation comes up.
mistakes: Using 매번 to mean 'every day' — that calendar meaning is 매일.
Adding a particle (매번에) — none is needed.

examples: I'll be there in a moment.
The food will be ready soon.
nuance: 금방 can mean both 'in a moment / very soon' (looking forward) and 'just now / a moment ago' (looking back), depending on the verb tense. With a future verb it means 'soon'; with a past verb it means 'just now'. It is very common and casual.
mistakes: Confusing 금방 (soon / just now) with 방금 (just now, only past). 방금 is strictly past.
Adding 에 — 금방 takes no particle.

examples: I kept studying / studied the whole time.
nuance: 계속 means an action keeps going without stopping ('continuously / keep ~ing'). It goes before the verb. Compare 자꾸, which means 'repeatedly / again and again' and often carries mild annoyance, while 계속 is just 'nonstop'.
mistakes: Using 계속 (nonstop) when you mean 'over and over' with a slight complaint — that nuance is 자꾸.
Saying 계속에 — no particle is used.

examples: I usually go to bed early.
There are more people than usual.
Today I went to work as usual.
nuance: 평소 means 'usual / normal times', and in everyday speech it is most often used as 평소에 ('usually') or in comparisons like 평소보다 ('than usual'). It describes your normal baseline, against which you can contrast today. 보통 is a close synonym for 'usually'.
mistakes: Forgetting the particle: for 'usually' the natural form is 평소에, not bare 평소.
Treating 평소 as a verb — it is a noun/time word, not an action.

examples: You will hear this in every shop.
We have no time, let's hurry and go.
nuance: 어서 urges someone to do something soon, but in a warm, welcoming way rather than a harsh 'hurry up'. You will hear 어서 오세요 ('welcome') constantly in stores and restaurants. It pairs naturally with polite commands like 오세요 and 드세요.
mistakes: Using 어서 as a sharp 'hurry up!' — it is gentle/welcoming; for blunt urgency use 빨리.
Confusing 어서 with 어서요 — add 요 only when used alone as a soft 'please go on'.

usage: A very short amount of time.
Polite way to ask for time.
nuance: 잠깐 means 'for a short moment / briefly'. It is everyday and conversational, and 잠깐만요 is one of the most useful phrases for asking someone to hold on. 잠시 is a slightly more formal synonym you will hear in announcements.
mistakes: Adding 에 (잠깐에) — it is an adverb and takes no particle.
Using 잠깐 for a long wait — it specifically means a very short time.

examples: We'll leave in a short while.
Let's rest here for a moment.
nuance: 잠시 means 'for a brief moment', very close to 잠깐 but a little more formal and polite. You hear it in public announcements (잠시 후에, 잠시만 기다려 주세요). In casual speech, 잠깐 is more common; 잠시 sounds a touch more refined.
mistakes: Thinking 잠시 and 잠깐 differ in meaning — they are the same; 잠시 is just more formal.
Saying 잠시에 — no particle; use 잠시 후에 or 잠시 동안 instead.

english: at first; for the first time
usage: Can act as a noun or time word.
examples: I came to Korea for the first time.
I'm eating this food for the first time.
nuance: 처음 means 'the first time' or 'the beginning'. As a time word it often appears as 처음에 ('at first') to contrast with how things are later, or as 처음으로 ('for the first time'). Its opposite is 마지막 (the last). You will meet it early in 처음 뵙겠습니다.
mistakes: Confusing 처음 (first / at first) with 먼저 (first in order, 'go ahead first'). They are not the same.
Forgetting 에 when you mean 'at first' — that nuance comes from 처음에.
